triples.head: Friedrich Miescher
triples.evidence: He named these chemicals (which would eventually be known as DNA) nuclein because they were isolated from the nuclei of the cells.

triples.head: Frederick Griffith
triples.evidence: British bacteriologist Frederick Griffith reported the first demonstration of bacterial transformation—a process in which external DNA is taken up by a cell, thereby changing its morphology and physiology.

triples.head: Frederick Griffith
triples.evidence: Griffith conducted his experiments with Streptococcus pneumoniae, a bacterium that causes pneumonia.

triples.head: Streptococcus pneumoniae
triples.evidence: The S strain is pathogenic (disease-causing), and has a capsule outside its cell wall.

triples.head: Oswald Avery
triples.evidence: They isolated the S strain from the dead mice and isolated the proteins and nucleic acids (RNA and DNA) as these were possible candidates for the molecule of heredity.

triples.head: DNA
triples.evidence: He called this the transforming principle (Figure 14.3).

triples.head: Martha Chase
triples.evidence: Chase and Hershey were studying a bacteriophage—a virus that infects bacteria.

triples.head: bacteriophage
triples.evidence: Viruses typically have a simple structure: a protein coat, called the capsid, and a nucleic acid core that contains the genetic material (either DNA or RNA).

triples.head: bacteriophage
triples.evidence: Viruses typically have a simple structure: a protein coat, called the capsid, and a nucleic acid core that contains the genetic material (either DNA or RNA).

triples.head: bacteriophage
triples.evidence: The bacteriophage infects the host bacterial cell by attaching to its surface, and then it injects its nucleic acids inside the cell.

triples.head: Martha Chase
triples.evidence: They labeled one batch of phage with radioactive sulfur, 35S, to label the protein coat.

triples.head: Martha Chase
triples.evidence: Another batch of phage were labeled with radioactive phosphorus, 32P.

triples.head: Martha Chase
triples.evidence: Hershey and Chase concluded that it was the phage DNA that was injected into the cell and carried information to produce more phage particles, thus providing evidence that DNA was the genetic material and not proteins (Figure 14.4).
